clue.text: Plain starter of meal daddy’s eating (6)

indicators.note: A starter is the first course, so what is wanted is only the opening letter of the word after it.
Whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so this word closes right round the letter before it.

blocks.note: daddy is papa, and papa's loses its apostrophe to become five plain letters
the first letter of meal, which is what a starter of it comes to

annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a father hogging the first course. Pampas grass is named after the plain it grows on, not the other way round, so the definition is the older sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain → PAMPAS: the treeless grass plain of Argentina and Uruguay, so a named flatland answers the general word for one.

clue.text: No place for pandemic, just fever (4)

indicators.note: Saying there is none of something is how a setter takes those letters out of the word that follows.

blocks.note: a plague is a disease sweeping a whole population
PL is the standing abbreviation for Place, as in a street name, and it is the pair that goes

annotation.walkthrough: The sentence reads as a hopeful bulletin — not a pandemic after all, only a temperature — and the reassurance is exactly the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: fever → AGUE: an old word for a shivering, malarial fever, kept alive now mainly by Shakespeare and crosswords.

clue.text: Whippersnapper very quietly suppressing single sound from mouse (9)

indicators.note: To suppress a thing is to hold it down and out of sight, so the letter named next is buried inside.

blocks.note: pp is pianissimo, the mark on a score telling a player to be very quiet
one, written as the Roman numeral
the noise a mouse makes

annotation.walkthrough: Two conventions worth banking do the front half: pp for pianissimo, and I for one. The mouse is the only ordinary English in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Whippersnapper → PIPSQUEAK: both are contemptuous names for somebody too young or too slight to be worth taking seriously.

clue.text: Appeared to do this from Nice beach? (6)

blocks.note: what you do on a beach, gazing out at the water
Nice sits on the French Riviera, and the water in front of it is the Med

annotation.walkthrough: Nice keeps its capital letter and its sand, which is the whole disguise: split the answer in two and it is what a holidaymaker there does all afternoon.
annotation.definitionFit: Appeared → SEEMED: 'she appeared calm' and 'she seemed calm' are the same past-tense verb of outward impression rather than fact.

clue.text: At court, a new sovereign (8)

indicators.note: Making a thing new means building it again out of the same materials, so the letters are laid down in another order.

blocks.note: eight letters, and every one of them is used

annotation.walkthrough: A royal court and a new sovereign make one smooth sentence, and every word of it except the indicator is raw material.
annotation.definitionFit: sovereign → AUTOCRAT: a sovereign is the ruler who answers to nobody, which is precisely the absolute power an autocrat holds.

clue.text: Contrary to inclination, objecting to Scotch? (7,3,5)

blocks.note: to object to a proposal is to be against it
grain whisky is one of the two kinds of Scotch, the other being malt; the question mark owns the leap

annotation.walkthrough: The comma is the join. One half is a plain synonym and the other reads the drink as a raw ingredient, which is the sort of leap a question mark always flags.
annotation.definitionFit: Contrary to inclination → AGAINST THE GRAIN: wood cuts cleanly one way only, so working the other way is the idiom for fighting a natural bent.

clue.text: Birds in most of the riverside plants (8)

indicators.note: Most of a word is all but a scrap of it, and the scrap left behind is the last letter.

blocks.note: most of THE, with its last letter dropped
rushes are the reeds that grow in the shallows at a river's edge

annotation.walkthrough: Song thrush, mistle thrush and blackbird are garden and woodland birds, never water birds, so the riverbank the clue paints is pure misdirection.
annotation.definitionFit: Birds → THRUSHES: one particular family of songbirds, so the answer sits inside the general plural as an example of it.

clue.text: Manage to get round small group of trees (5)

indicators.note: To get round something is to pass all the way about it, so these letters close on either side of the next piece.

blocks.note: to cope with a job is to manage it
S is the label on the smallest shirt on the rail

annotation.walkthrough: S for small comes off the clothes rail and is worth banking: setters reach for it constantly when a container needs a single letter inside.
annotation.definitionFit: group of trees → COPSE: a copse is a small thicket, the coppiced wood that was cut back for poles and left to sprout again.

clue.text: Move cat aside, keeping very connected (10)

indicators.note: To move a thing is to take it out of the position it was in, which is what happens to every letter here.
What you keep you hold on to and carry along, so this extra pair travels into the mix with the rest.

blocks.note: eight of the ten letters come from here
so means very — 'not so bad' — and its two letters make the count up

annotation.walkthrough: 'Move the cat aside' is a sentence anybody might say, and none of it survives: the animal is only letters, and 'very' is hiding a two-letter word.
annotation.definitionFit: connected → ASSOCIATED: two things associated with one another are linked in fact or in memory, the sense used in 'associated company'.

clue.text: Having cooked bean soup, one requires attendance (8)

definitions.note: The answer is a noun and the definition is what it does: the setter names the document by the demand it makes, with 'one' standing in for the document itself.

indicators.note: Whatever goes in the pot comes out changed past recognition, so the letters are served up in a new order.

blocks.note: B, E, A, N, S, O, U, P — the eight letters, with nothing added

annotation.walkthrough: The Latin is worth knowing: sub poena, 'under penalty', which is what makes the summons an order rather than an invitation.
annotation.definitionFit: requires attendance → SUBPOENA: the court order compelling a witness to turn up, so the answer is the thing that does the requiring.

clue.text: Take another attitude to rest (6)

blocks.note: an attitude is a pose, so taking a fresh one is to pose again
this half asks for a word meaning to rest or lie at ease, usable as noun or verb

annotation.walkthrough: The split is at 'to', and the hyphen a grid cannot show is the whole clue: two different words happen to be spelt the same way.
annotation.definitionFit: Repose is rest or stillness in the plain sense, and read as re-pose it is striking a fresh attitude, since an attitude is a pose held.

clue.text: Once Standard English no longer heard at opening of Parliament (6,6)

definitions.text: Once Standard English no longer heard at opening of Parliament

blocks.clueFragment: Once Standard English no longer heard
blocks.note: The surface is the familiar grumble that nobody at Westminster speaks properly any more, with 'Standard English' as the grammarian's term for the correct form.
The setter means the State Opening, where the monarch reads out the government's programme — and what that address is called depends on who is on the throne.

annotation.walkthrough: Nothing separates into letters here. Both halves lean on the same possessive: the monarch's English was the yardstick, the monarch's address opens Parliament, and a king ended both phrases.
annotation.definitionFit: The address the sovereign reads at the State Opening is named for whoever delivers it, so it belonged to Elizabeth II and belongs now to Charles.

clue.text: Killer’s destiny in being caught by subterfuge (10)

indicators.note: Whatever is caught is held fast inside the thing that caught it, so these letters shut around the ones before.

blocks.note: guile is cunning, the deceiver's stock in trade
your lot is what fate has handed you
the preposition is taken at face value, for its own two letters

annotation.walkthrough: The word doing least work on the surface is doing most underneath: 'in' looks like grammar and is really two letters of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Killer → GUILLOTINE: the beheading machine of the French Revolution, named after Dr Guillotin, so the definition names it by its trade.

clue.text: Slippery equine? (4)

definitions.note: 'Slippery' is not the adjective it looks like: the setter means 'of the slipper sort', and the question mark owns the coinage.

blocks.note: this half names a backless slipper, the kind you step into rather than put on
the offspring of a donkey and a mare

annotation.walkthrough: Two words and a question mark, which is where the difficulty lives: with no wordplay to unpick, the only lever is that question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: equine → MULE: a donkey and mare cross; and the same word names a backless slipper, which is the sense hidden in 'Slippery'.

clue.text: 18 on a course that is dry (8)

blocks.note: every hole on a golf course is driven off from a tee
eighteen holes means eighteen of them, so the number is the tally

annotation.walkthrough: Split the answer into two words and the clue is a fact about golf: count the tees on a full round and eighteen is what you get.
annotation.definitionFit: dry → TEETOTAL: 'dry' is what a county or a wedding is called when no alcohol is served, and a teetotaller serves none either.

clue.text: Alumni’s pub evening is a thing! (9)

blocks.note: a school's alumni are its old boys, and OB is how the school magazine writes it
a session is a drinker's own word for an evening spent at it

annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark is the setter grinning: 'is a thing' only became a definition in the last twenty years, and the clue is written in that register throughout.
annotation.definitionFit: a thing → OBSESSION: in the casual 'he has a thing about tidiness', a thing is exactly a fixation, which is what an obsession is.

clue.text: Initial contribution to thread that gives clear directions (8)

definitions.note: The answer is a noun and the definition says what it does; 'that' turns the phrase into a description of the object rather than a synonym for it.

blocks.note: to initial a form is to sign it — the verb, not the letter
a message added to an online thread is a post

annotation.walkthrough: 'Initial' looks exactly like an instruction to take a first letter, which is the one thing it is not doing here. Read it as a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: gives clear directions → SIGNPOST: the fingerpost at a junction spells out which road leads where, so the object is named by its job.

clue.text: Typically male slob struggling with hike (8)

indicators.note: Anything struggling is thrashing about and will not hold still, so its letters do not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: four of the eight letters
and the other four

annotation.walkthrough: The surface shows a man wrestling a rucksack up a hill, and the two nouns either side of the indicator are the only material in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Typically male → BLOKEISH: a bloke is British slang for an ordinary man, so blokeish behaviour is the stereotypically masculine kind.

clue.text: Drop tools here (4)

blocks.note: trees let their leaves fall away each year, and snakes do the same with their skin
the hut at the end of the garden, named by what is kept in it

annotation.walkthrough: Three words and no wordplay at all. The surface is an instruction to down tools, and the split comes after the very first word.
annotation.definitionFit: Drop → SHED: a tree drops its leaves by shedding them; and a shed is the garden hut, defined the second time by its contents.

clue.text: Relax on firm topper on mattress for programme (6)

indicators.note: A topper goes on top of what it names, and the top of a word is the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: to sit down is to take the weight off
CO is company, the abbreviation on any letterhead
the first letter of mattress, the end a topper covers

annotation.walkthrough: Sitcom is short for situation comedy, and the clue never mentions comedy at all — the definition works at the widest level it can get away with.
annotation.definitionFit: programme → SITCOM: a situation comedy is a television programme, so the general word names it by its slot in the schedules.

clue.text: Tense morning working for Europeans (12)

indicators.note: Something working is in motion rather than at rest, so the letters will not stay where the clue set them down.

blocks.note: twelve letters, which is the length of the answer

annotation.walkthrough: Balkan nationalities are a setter's friend: long, and stocked with the vowels and common consonants an anagram needs to hide inside an ordinary phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Europeans → MONTENEGRINS: the people of Montenegro, an Adriatic state in the Balkans, so one nation stands as an example of the continent.

clue.text: Securing hearing without resistance (5)

indicators.note: Here the word means lacking rather than outside, so what follows it is missing from the piece before.

blocks.note: a case being heard in court is being tried, so a hearing is a trying
R is the physicist's symbol for resistance, and it is the letter that goes

annotation.walkthrough: Court and courtroom are never mentioned, so the step to find is that a hearing and a trying are the same event seen from two benches.
annotation.definitionFit: Securing → TYING: making a thing fast with a knot is one way of securing it, and both are -ing forms of the verb.

clue.text: Enthusiasm in the heart of Commonwealth country (4)

indicators.note: The heart of a thing is dead centre, so the letters wanted are the middle ones and both ends are left off.

blocks.note: the country is New Zealand, and reading its two words as one continuous string, the wanted letters sit exactly in the middle, three trimmed from each end

annotation.walkthrough: The country is never named, only described, so the work is finding a Commonwealth member with a whole word parked at its middle.
annotation.definitionFit: Enthusiasm → ZEAL: zeal is enthusiasm with conviction behind it, the word English keeps for religious and political fervour.

clue.text: Try to stop celebrity endlessly showing sexual urge (6)

indicators.note: A dentist stops a tooth by filling the hole in it, so one word is packed into the middle of another.
Something endless has no end, so the final letter of the word is not there to be written down.

blocks.note: a celebrity is a lion — the lion of the season, the guest everyone wants — with its tail letter gone
a bid is an attempt: a bid for freedom

annotation.walkthrough: Lion for a celebrity is Victorian drawing-room English, the literary lion of the season, and it is that sense the clue needs rather than the animal.
annotation.definitionFit: sexual urge → LIBIDO: Freud's term for the drive behind sexual desire, now the everyday word for how much of it somebody has.

clue.text: Old records from accomplished country singer (8)

blocks.note: arch means chief of its kind, as in arch-enemy, so an arch practitioner is a thorough one
Burl Ives, who sang Big Rock Candy Mountain

annotation.walkthrough: A surname alone, with no first name offered, is the setter's standing notice that you are looking for a well-known person rather than a word.
annotation.definitionFit: Old records → ARCHIVES: an archive is an institution's store of historic documents, so the plural names the old papers themselves.

clue.text: Raise the hinge that’s wonky (8)

indicators.note: Something wonky sits askew instead of true, so the letters are set down crooked rather than in their proper order.

blocks.note: eight letters, including the article, which the setter needs for its E

annotation.walkthrough: The article is fodder, which is the thing to spot: 'the' looks like grammar and is carrying two of the answer's letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Raise → HEIGHTEN: to heighten is to make higher, and both verbs stretch from lifting a wall to sharpening tension or colour.

clue.text: Make a mess of motorway gradient (6)

blocks.note: M is the letter Britain puts on its motorway numbers, the M1 and the M25
the angle of a slope is its gradient

annotation.walkthrough: A mangle was the pair of rollers that wrung the water out of washing, and anything fed through one came out flat — which is where the modern sense comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: Make a mess of → MANGLE: to mangle a tune or a name is to botch it so thoroughly that it comes out barely recognisable.
